Chapter 3: Giving Clear Feedback and Recognizing Strengths
So, once you’ve built trust—by really being present and listening closely—the next step is all about giving feedback that actually helps.
Now, a lot of folks hear the word “feedback” and instantly think, “Uh oh, criticism’s coming…” But what if you could shift that mindset?
True feedback isn’t about pointing out what’s wrong—it’s a tool for growth and, honestly, a way to show someone you see them. When it’s done right, feedback lets people know where they stand, what they’re doing great, and where there’s room to get even better.
Here’s something to pay attention to: for feedback to really land, it needs to be specific and timely.
Think about it—if someone just says, “Good job,” or, “That wasn’t great,” it’s pretty hard to know what to keep doing or what to change.
Instead, focus feedback on things you can actually see—behaviors, results, actions—so it’s easy for the person to connect the dots.
Imagine feedback as a mirror. A good mirror doesn’t stretch or shrink your reflection—it just shows you what’s really there.
That’s what effective feedback does. It gives a clear, honest picture—highlighting both the strengths and the areas where someone can grow.
So, what makes feedback truly effective? Let’s break it down:
First, focus on what someone did—not who they are.
Second, be specific about what you noticed and what impact it had.
Third, try to balance positive recognition with suggestions for improvement.
And finally, don’t wait too long—share feedback close to when the event happened.
Recognition is just as important as pointing out what needs work.
People naturally want to repeat things that get noticed and appreciated.
Public recognition can boost the whole team’s morale, but even a private word or a handwritten note can mean a lot to someone.
Let me share a quick example. In a busy hospital, a nurse manager made a habit of recognizing team members who went above and beyond for their patients.
Sometimes it was a simple thank-you, sometimes just a note or a quick shout-out at a meeting.
Over time, this small commitment to recognition led to happier staff and fewer people leaving the team.
Now, that doesn’t mean you can ignore tough conversations.
If someone’s performance isn’t where it needs to be, it’s important to address it directly—but always with empathy, and with a focus on how to move forward, not just what went wrong.
Here’s a practical way to approach feedback:
Start with something positive to show your support.
Clearly lay out the behavior or outcome that you want to talk about.
Invite the other person to share their thoughts.
And then, work together on next steps—whether it’s improvement, or building on what’s already working.
When feedback becomes a regular, everyday part of team life—rather than something rare or dreaded—it completely changes the culture.
People start to see feedback as a gift, not a threat.
So, here’s the key takeaway: giving clear feedback and recognizing strengths are some of the best ways to lift others up.
It helps people see their value, shows them how to grow, and keeps them motivated to give their best.
And when you combine these habits with deep listening, you create a powerful force for growth—for both individuals and the whole team.
